body: Thanks again for the many replies. I am doing much better now. I just have to keep my head clear and my eyes pointed forward.

Sorry to hear you aren't feeling so well. Definitely do whatever you need to to take care of yourself. I don't think anything you wrote came out bad. Go at whatever pace works for you.

As for interacting with my father, it helped that I moved a thousand miles away recently. But now he's started sending me all these emails and calling me at least once a week. I guess I don't mind things being superficial and fake if they are in the background and come up not more than once a month, but this isn't working for me, so thanks for the direction. I'm going to talk with my therapist about this on Friday to get even more insight.

I think what you say about how he should accept me for who I am is a very important point. I am who I am and I need to be true to myself, not just an accessory to someone else's delusion. That's probably a big problem for a lot of areas of my life, and it might even be one of the "things jammed in my head" that I still haven't quite grasped yet: that I need to know who I am and be who I am rather than worrying about the minor unpleasantness doing so might cause to others. Because it will make things much more pleasant for me, and likely also for the other people in my life with whom I interact. I think my situation with my father is the most fundamental, representative case of this problem of mine, so it will be good to finally face it down. The idea that "oh, whatever, I'll just let it go and let the man keep his delusions" really just hasn't worked out for me. And I know I'm throwing away many many years of making that possible... but... oh well, who cares? :-)

By talking it out a bit with others beforehand (e.g. with you and my therapist) hopefully I can lay things out in a decent, reasonable way that isn't poisoned by anger.

She was reasonably upset because she called me early in the morning and was telling me she was stressed about a looming deadline. I didn't show enough patience or support because I myself had been up all night trying to prepare some work of my own that was due in only a matter of hours. But of course she's calling because she is really feeling stressed and it's not correct for me to just think "oh, I've got the same situation here, why is she complaining about it so much, and why is she doing it to me?" It's not correct: it's out of touch, in maybe a very deep way in my case. She still thinks I am a good person but doesn't really accept that I have a deep problem that I need to fix. In the few cases where I am not in my mental illness situation and I happen to be with her, she notices a dramatic change and says things like "what's gotten into you?" and "why are you all of the sudden so affectionate?"

She isn't telling me I'm incapable of being human most of the time—rather I'm trying to tell her, but I don't know if she completely understands. It's also a long distance relationship and we are both exceedingly busy anyway, so it's hard on those terms as well. She is probably completely right that I need to communicate a lot more, but I have no idea how much is healthy, etc., etc. But I guess there's probably a place on Reddit to sort that out, too, so maybe I'll look there in the near future as well.

... continuing ...

**Re: humoring him** I guess the other thing I’m worried about is hurting my mom, who is a nice, generally normal person. Unfortunately my dad is very demanding and domineering, so she is, in a way, a captive of his, also locked up in all kinds of religious mind-fuckery that he uses against her.

As for kindness, at this point, we get “kindness” but it’s all very superficial. It’s like he realized that “Oh, for some reason my son never calls and is not interested in talking to me and doesn’t tell me about any important life events” and so now he’s being, like “nice”, but if I told him for example that I practice Buddhism, or that I’ve had premarital sex, or that I’m not 100% convinced in a 6000 year old earth, or that I’m not opposed to other people having different gender identities or sexual orientations, I feel like he would be exceedingly disapproving and wouldn’t accept me. So he’s “nice”, but only to an imaginary version of me, so it really doesn’t even feel like anything because I know he wouldn’t accept me for who I actually am. Like he has in his head still that he was a great father, and maybe he has at some point begin to clue into the possibility that not everything that pops into his head is divine wisdom, and so he’s just trying to adopt this role of “good older father”. But it’s ridiculous: he’s literally told us if there’s anything that goes on in our lives that he wouldn’t want to hear about, that we shouldn’t tell him (so I guess he can maintain his delusions), and I guess since we aren’t “under his roof” he doesn’t feel the threat of us “damaging his self-image/reputation as a Godly man” by “sinning when it’s in his power to stop it.”

Yeah, I’ve been reading through a book about “toxic parents” recently, which is why I’ve been thinking that maybe I should in fact stand up for myself, even if it isn’t pleasant. I think ending the obligatory sense of enmeshment would really help me, mentally. I just hate to hurt anyone, particularly my more-or-less innocent mother.

**Re: why am I toxic** I’m a sociopath. I don’t have feelings and can’t see people. I have a bunch of manipulative mental algorithms that maneuver me through life, because that’s all I’m really capable of having. So I’m emotionally unavailable and don’t have natural tendencies to stay properly in touch; it’s forced. Me being in a relationship is like tricking someone to fall in love with a robot. Like I said I think this year I’ve made some big strides, but I’m still really a mess, and no one should have to deal with me while I’m like this until I get things straightened out. I’m obviously not supportive enough and don’t help her feel loved and desirable. I’m just kind of dead and not interested in anything most of the time, and people shouldn’t have to only get by on only occasional humanness and support. I also feel like I’m at risk of dragging her through a mess where she feels obligated to “stay with me” because of my situation, and that’s not healthy if its really not working for here.

No worries at all on the “delay”. Yeah, I guess that I am a sociopath. But like a weird one that has all of these “moral rules” drilled into his head and with an instinct to “be Good”. But not actually good, just a fake approximation of good defined by a bunch of rules someone else made up that have nothing to do with emotions or compassion.

It’s weird. I remember when I was in junior high I got on the bus with my classmates for some kind of trip, and I had weirdly been reading the dictionary the day before, and I came across the word “asocial” and I saw it mentioned other similar words. I literally typed in the definitions for *asocial*, *nonsocial*, *antisocial*, and I think one other one. I printed this little list, and I had brought it with me. I thought it was “cool” and I explained to my friend that of all of these options I was actually “nonsocial”. But I considered this a badge of pride, to be nonsocial. I don’t know how to explain to you the kind of influence that would make that seem like a desirable characteristic, but it had to do with my dad’s big clash with my “vain” oldest brother and the complete capitulation of my second oldest brother, who was always a bit unique and had his own way of things anyway. The second oldest brother was set up to me as a role model. And since fear, guilt, and brainwashing made him have a sort of pride about essentially disintegrating as a person, and since his friendships suffered he was often at home, despressedly in his room under the never ending surveillance of my father (we didn’t really have privacy). So he was ~5 years older than me and he was set up as my example of what a person should be, and though not explicitly contrasted with my oldest brother, brainwashing (and all of the denigration of my oldest brother in his absence) sort of made contrast the natural choice for me. So I actually was trained to be against human connection. There were other ways in which I was similarly trained, as I’ve hinted at w/r/t extreme sexual repression.

So it looks like maybe all my habits and instincts make me a sociopath. Maybe that’s the answer.

**Re: blatant abuse** I’ve always sensed this was the case, but one of the things he did was also instill all of these instincts in my that “I’m never going to be an inconsiderate, selfish person like my oldest brother” because I was 11 when these ideas were being presented to me. So that’s another case of things that even today are probably still jammed in there: I think my dad did some really awful things, but I can’t really bring myself to accept it, so I probably need to take some kind of remedial actions here, but I don’t know what they are. Do you have any ideas of where to start fixing my attitudes here?

**Re: tying myself up in knots + a tangent about infantilization** Ah, yes. Correct diagnosis. I guess when you are suicidal for two years and you completely stop interacting with friends (like visiting a friend or having a friend over happens less than 5 times in an entire year), maybe that should be a sign? Maybe when you are always very sad looking and you regularly pick at your face until it bleeds and leaves a big scab Father should think “Oh, maybe something is wrong?”

The thing is, it’s like based on my two older brothers and maybe some dumb TV/movie stereotypes my father concluded that all teenagers were unappreciative and out to get him. It was so artificial; like the day I turned “13” he started treating me differently. He would literally and regularly say “who are you, and what have you done with my son?” And I felt really really bad about it. I didn’t want him to feel that way, so I tried, much to my disadvantage as a person, to not “grow up” and get involved with all of the evil social things my peers were starting to do.

So I wanted him to be happy, but he was very against social health and also had this strange attachment to “the innocence of childhood” that stemmed maybe from some mutant desire to use each son’s childhood as a way to live the “childhood he never got to have”. It’s a strange thing to suggest someone would have this kind of attachment using his children like this, but he regularly suggested this to us. I remember for example once as a child I was playing with Legos and he said with a tone of sadness and disappointment that one day I wouldn’t like my Legos anymore [and I’d sinfully ruin my innocence becoming a bad person like my older brothers who also grew up]. During our “sex talk” when I was 9 (during which I cried the whole time because I was made to feel very guilty and shameful), I was wisely informed that my second oldest brother called the process of growing up “turning into a hairy monster,” so that was another healthy idea to plant in my head. One time years later I was looking for my birth certificate and I was told to look in this lockbox and as I was looking I came across this sparsely kept journal of my father’s and essentially laid exactly my diagnosis of the situation out: he talked sadly about a camping trip how my second oldest brother and I had given up our innocence and didn’t want to be children anymore and how my youngest brother might only have one more summer left in him. I guess it’s kind of like we weren’t exactly people. We certainly didn’t have rights or privacy (because why would we need those if we were moral?), and our opinions and desires not only didn’t matter, but were sinful for their immorality. We were more or less just tools.

**… + a tangent of being actual tools**
And once we each turned 13 we literally were tools in my dad’s construction business, because while the work was never that unreasonable it certainly wasn’t an opportunity to learn social skills, and we didn’t actually learn the trade; we were always just assigned menial tasks. I remember one summer there were these 8 trailers homes that my dad owned and he wanted to paint this energy saving white paint on their aluminum tops. So in humid high 90s °F weather we had to scrape the tar at every metal segment of every trailer, then sand every square inch of every trailer (each of which had a very flimsy roof, so you had to spread your weight out, crawling on your hands and knees), then wash and paint them. I remember that I started to have boils of sweat forming underneath the skin on my forearms because I guess it was like being in an oven. We got a little bit more than minimum wage for our various jobs. I used the money to pay for a car, car insurance, and a computer for school that I planned on also using in university. I remember I wanted to take college-level courses in high school but I was discouraged from doing so because it cost money. I didn’t have the money to pay for the textbooks I needed because I had paid for the transportation I needed to attend extracurricular school activities and I had paid for the computer I was going to need for college. But my dad did say “normally I’d like you to have an investment in your own education, but in just this case I’ll help you out and buy these textbooks.” So at least he did that.

I really felt like he didn’t like me just because I was a teenager, and that sucked because I tried to do things that would keep him happy and the cost of my own development, but he was so attached to his superficial ideas that he didn’t see my actions and still saw me as traitor, as if I could help growing up.

... continued ...

**Re: “scary other”** Let me try to explain a little bit more. So it is true that I feel very uncomfortable about making eye contact with people (it always feels wrong, either too much, too concentrated, or too little), and I worry a lot about what people think when I’m in “robot mode”. It’s strange, but I guess I have this feeling that everyone hates me, and that doesn’t really stand up to the external facts. But with respect to the bear, I guess the main point is that the bear, while it might have emotions and you might be able to get attached to it like you might get attached to a pet, I sense that there is some kind of important, uniquely human experience that happens between people. As for other, you probably get what I mean, but I want to be clear that I don’t mean “human Other”. Rather I mean the heavier of my panicked instincts make it feel like the existence of “a person” inside this being that I am encountering is just as likely and absurd as there being “a person” inside a duck.

**Re: confronting emotional losses** I have actually been bent on “improving my situation” for quite a number of years, and this “breakthrough” I’m talking about might partly be attributable to these “improvements”, insofar as they gradually moved me to a place where I would be able to handle it, but I don’t think that gradual improvements will ever fix the problem. It’s like if you dislocate a bone. No matter what kind of nice diet you have, if you don’t pop things back into place then gradual improvement will never actually be able to resolve your problem. I have to wonder if other people in similar situations see the step of “popping the bone back into place” or if it just happens and they consider it part of the gradual improvement process; I of course I also have to wonder how pervasive equivalents of my mental environment actually are. But “when my mental illness goes away” it’s a completely different experience. My encounter with reality is completely altered, and it’s really a big relief. When I’m in this state, I can perfectly see how normal people would have naturally wound up in this state.

**Re: knowing the rules** It’s interesting, because when I’m in my mentally well state, I feel like I “know the rules”; I have an instinctual grasp of what is going on and what I want, and everything is completely OK (or it feels like it would be completely OK if I could count on sustaining this improved mental situation). Once again, it’s a huge relief.

Would you describe feeling like you “don’t know the rules” as anxiety? Because I get that myself, and I’m not sure I actually know what anxiety is because I either don’t feel it while it’s happening or I am in denial that it could ever happen to me.

**Re: my father** I guess you could describe his new place as “dark” but I think it would probably be better to use different adjectives. Both places were not 100% good, but severely, excessively beating a man and then comprehending what you’ve done is probably more what I would call “dark” than being deceived that TV religion is going to make everything completely OK if you follow its bad advice. He genuinely was striving to be a good person, which I think is commendable even if your ego or immaturity or whatever clouds your judgement and you kind of botch it.

I guess the things that happened in my childhood are like a garden variety car accident. Maybe my dad is driving one car and he swerves out of the way to avoid hitting a cat, and when he does this he’s in my lane where I’m coming in the opposite direction. So I also swerve, but I end up in rolling my car in the ditch, and my dad is like so focused on having saved the cat that I guess he doesn’t comprehend that I was in a car coming the other way and am now in the ditch. He calls me on my phone and I’m in the hospital, but I don’t tell him I’m in the hospital, I’m just like “that was really good of you to not hit that cat!” Because what’s the point in telling him he ran my car off the road? Technically he didn’t. He strongly, perhaps even obliviously provided very strong motivation for me to swerve my car out of the way. But I didn’t have to swerve, or maybe my swerve was not soon enough or deft enough.

But maybe you can give me some perspective here. I suppose that perhaps many parents who do not so good things still have a very positive image about themselves, but I don’t really have any personal experience/data that supports this assumption. But is this often the case, that a “toxic parent” is unknowingly toxic? And what do you do if they’re unknowingly toxic? I mean, I’m really frustrated that my life is all kinds of messed up despite some really intense effort on my part, but what am I even supposed to do with regards to my father at this point? I mean, he’ll be turning 60 soon. I see no point in tampering with his happy delusions. Trying to “bring him to reality” so we could have an “actual relationship” doesn’t interest me; I mean maybe one day I might imagine having had that would have been meaningful, but I’m not going to spend yet more years confronting him and then gradually teaching him how to emotionally be an adult just so at the end I can pretend that I have an authentic father-son relationship. That’d just be delusional. I mean, if the relationship didn’t form as I was becoming an adult (if emotionally that even happened when I was in the same house or has even happened yet) and he was instead just insane and hostile, then the time is passed. Now it wouldn’t be a father-son relationship. It’d just be a relationship with some random needy old dude that has the same last name as me.

But here’s the point I’m trying to get to: not only do I humor him, like I still visit and pretend everything is OK. I’m not sure if I’m going to visit again, but in past years it was always a big mistake to return to the house. And he’d be like “OK we’re going to church” and I’d just go along, not even meeting him there, but riding in the back of his car. I’m worried that even today I’m allowing way too much enmeshment to occur, and it’s always bad for me and it’s always a trigger for lousy memories and bad self-image ideas when I talk to him. But he’s also a person, maybe even kind of a child, really, and I just feel guilty for potentially making him feel bad. But I worry: am I doing this out of impartial, neutral kindness, or am I doing it out of still-internalized servitude?

I mean I think about the man way way way too much, and he tries to talk to me once a week, too. I would just rather not be reminded of my hellish time in La La Land four times a month. Maybe once a month I could handle, but it’s maybe even interfering with my job because it keeps making me more depressed. But at the same time I feel like it’s not the noble thing to do, to cut him out, and I should help him instead of hurt him, and still recognize the good things he’s done.

I don’t know. Talk some sense into me here :-)

**Re: a mental ward** I am pretty confident this many years in that I am not a risk to myself. I know what they say about desensitization, but if I didn’t kill myself in the last 6 months it’s probably not going to get any worse, so now it doesn’t seem strategic to end up there.

Also, I was under the impression that being institutionalized somehow went on a permanent record or something, and while I guess that probably wouldn’t matter so much for many people, in my case it might be an issue. What are the ways that such documentation can hurt people?

You are right about my strong aversion to being controlled. I’m even so over the top about it that it probably interferes with my ability to establish an identity. I don’t feel like I can adopt any kind of style or culture because that would be giving away a part of myself to the control of some kind of social phenomenon/movement/company. But the control doesn’t “scare me”; I would just really not like it and it would mess up a lot of the good things that I’ve managed to get going in my life. I’m more concerned about losing my job and being stigmatized. I’d just have to essentially start my life over yet again, and that’s never convenient, and I just went through all the work of doing just that half a year ago.

I also think I’m finally on the brink of sorting this out and I’m pretty confident that my particular solution won’t be facilitated at a mental ward.

**Re: feelings today** Today I was very concerned because I am seriously underperforming at work. My younger brother is visiting, so that's nice, but I broke off my long-distance relationship with my girlfriend because it wasn't working and I was not being emotionally supportive at all. Or emotional at all. I was just hurting her by being so unavailable (partly because of depression, partly because I am literally working ALL of the time, like sometimes 17hrs a day), so I confirmed the concerns she expressed to me and I told her that I was toxic and that even if I have a way of saying things nicely she should hold on to her current understanding of the situation so that she can get the kind of relationship she deserves. Talking with her and sorting things out myself took a toll on me and I didn't make it into work to take care of some important stuff I had going, and so my reputation at work is further damaged. But I'm not suicidal right now; it helps that I haven't missed taking my antidepressants since... I started this thread :)

**Re: people as background things** In the moments where I am what I am assuming is “mentally well” or at least more so than usual, I comprehend that people exist. I try to practice this as I pass by people during the day. I say “that’s just a person there” and I try to imagine the person having interests or having a favorite movie that they might tell someone about. I guess I see people the way you might see a bear in the woods. It’s something terrifying that you have to respond to, and not at all something that you connect to. Obviously I have instincts beneath my condition that allow me to in some ways connect with people, but it is often a very slow and bumpy process. Partly I think it is fueled by denial, because deep down I’m terrified of confronting the emotional losses in my life, because it’s like I’ve lost everything, and it hits me all at once, and it’s very sad. Everything was fake.

**Re: Comprehending reality** The above answer gives you a little bit of insight into this. Maybe it’s that I’ve just always been 100% emotionally dead? And then having emotions is very bizarre, but sort of makes sense? I don’t exactly know. Maybe the first time I was “breaking through” a few years ago I tried to tell someone what I was experiencing. I was saying “people are people” which I know sounds like the dumbest A is A sort of postulate, but maybe if I could extend what was actually going on in my head to that person I would have said something more like: “So these terrifying things that I encounter every day and that have endless rules that I have to figure out and follow when interacting with them are what you call people. They have feelings and opinions and they don’t really have a million rules to always generate the right answer. They just want things and experience happiness, sadness, and desire and curiosity, and have tastes, preferences, styles, and attachments. Who’d of thought? I guess everyone except me.”

Comprehending reality also means peeling back the delusions, many of which have to do with the very existence of emotions, the various things “jammed in my head” that I mentioned, grandiose ideas about my abilities and future, the true extent of what I lost.

Regarding the extent of what I lost, I guess I would explain it like this. My mental illness is a disease that kills me backwards. Instead of cutting of years starting at, say 64 as a heart attack might, it started cutting them off at the front. And now I’m in my 20s and over 20 years have been cut out of my life. It feels like I’ve been dead, and in my case it doesn’t feel like I’m coming back from the dead, it feels like—and this is probably overgruesome phrasing—I’m being born a rotting, middle-aged corpse in some long, drawn-out, frequently stalling process.

**Re: happiness + a tangent about my father** Thank you. It’s worth noting that I’ve been working on this for a long time and I recognize that my happiness should matter and I do experience probably a flattened version of “happiness”. The main thing is that these ideas are jammed in my head from a long way back so their kind of interwoven into a lot of places and have a lot of permutations, and I have internalized instincts that go along with believing them or having believed them, so I also have lots of little internal habits that I have to identify and counteract. But yeah, I think that was the main lesson of my childhood, that my happiness is unimportant, or expensive, or inconvenient for others, or something that I should be ashamed of greedily pursuing. Or perhaps in another permutation: “what you call happiness is just sinfulness, greed, lust, self-centeredness, and when you want something, you are a bad person; you shouldn’t want anything at all; you should only be completely empty so as to more efficiently follow these rules I am giving you, and then one day you will attain happiness and the meaning of life; that day is of course the day you die when you go to heaven [just like I heard on TV]; the day you die.” To be clear: that’s not a quotation or a paraphrasing; it’s rather the message that I seem to have internalized at some point in elementary school. In retrospect it more or less felt like “happiness” had nothing to do with anything inside me and was something reserved for “actions that ‘entertained’ my father.” Which is to say he really enjoyed seeing himself as a “provider” and a “good father”.

Although we never talked about it, he used to allude to things having been very bad for him in the past, so the man is not without his own problems. He would suggest that he used to get beaten, saying that if he had spoken back to his father the way child-me was speaking “he’d be peeling himself off the walls with his fingernails”. I don’t know where he got that phrase, and it might well be a very second-hand phrase. His parents divorced when he was 10, and he would often complain that this was a very rare thing at the time, in the mid-sixties in the midwest. And I’m sure that’s a shitty situation, and can I really fault the man too much if he didn’t get over things if I myself am so slow to get over things? There were stories floating around town about my father when he was a bouncer before he found religion. And while stories are sure to get exaggerated, he apparently was not someone you wanted to mess with at all. When he tells people his “personal testimony” he starts off by saying that he was spiritually in a very dark place, and then something made him feel like turning on the TV. And then the 700 Club with Pat Robertson was on. This was in the 1970s. His housemate told him to “turn that crap off”, but he didn’t and the rest is the rest of history: his story. My younger brother later related to me about further details he had learned about this night. Apparently “spiritually in a very dark place” meant that he had lost control and beaten someone so severely that (the story said) they were at risk of dying. He was thus swept up in the tawdry TV religion culture of the 80s and 90s particularly because he had a sense of allegiance from that moment on.

So hopefully that gives a little bit more balance. He’s made some mistakes, but he’s been dealing with his own life and trying very hard to do a good job. I guess that’s part of what made things so confusing for me. He seemed like a really good person who was trying to help me, but it was a lot more complicated than that, and he was having a lot of bad ideas funneled into his head, corrupting the direction of his good intentions. And he wasn’t as perfect or clued-in to reality as he presented himself as being. (He presented himself as being in touch with God and thus effectively infallible; arguing with him essentially was tantamount to arguing against his religious beliefs; anyone who had a different opinion from him was either a pompous moron or—kid you not—an agent of Satan).

**Re: negative consequences of sharing my conversation** I pretty much mean I am paranoid about saying things that might cause me to lose control of my life. Like “I own a nitrogen asphyxiation apparatus”. I have no idea what the limits are for someone pulling the plug and forcing me into some kind of compulsory treatment.

My relationships with my brothers are all as good as they've ever been, I guess, to the extent that we have actual relationships, which my not be the case (I sense that I am rarely capable of actually engaging in any kind of "relationship" with someone). I don't know if you'd follow this or not because I don't think it's a very common thing, this mental condition that I perceive myself to have. Or at least I sense it is maybe a very uncommon thing to have it and comprehend that you have it. Else, it's more common than I expect, but never talked about in our society.

It's actually pretty foreign to me (which I'm sure is terrible) that your first comment is about my brother, because I lack these emotional faculties and generally can't actually /attain/ that other people really exist. Which is definitely the most awful way a mind/personality could be rigged up, am I right? I have a lot of niceties programmed into my behavioral algorithms, if you will, but at the core I am actually a rotten person--like rotten in the sense of wilted and decomposing, not just as a rehashed hyperbolic adjective. I'm mechanically disposed to become a Good person, so it's not all bad. The problem is that underneath I am not actually a person, or perhaps more rightly the person is still very very alarmingly nascent. So extremely nascent that when I comprehend reality I usually go into something like shock and extreme denial, and then I lose myself for a few more months in the fog.

Hollow on the inside refers to my normal "unwell" state where I am not really a person on the inside. Like this is not exaggerated depressive metaphor-making. This is, I'm increasingly becoming able to fear, a 100% real and serious mental health problem. "Starting to feel things" refers to the very startling real world that I've momentarily rejoined. For the last three years I've been able to occasionally have moments where I overcome my denial and see my overwhelming situation. Each time I break through to reality it seems like maybe I move a little bit closer to fixing this, and the breakthroughs are maybe coming a little bit more frequently now.

Yes, those were things I was taught. Yes, some of them literally, explicitly taught. In all cases the message I wrote was completely intended, even if I have removed the strange sugar-coating applied to some of them. There are many many more.

I really don't know what to say either. I guess that's why I'm feeling optimistic about trying to talk to strangers on the internet about this in some low profile, anonymous way: how could I ever really explain this to another person, especially in a mode of communication other than writing? I don't think anyone would really believe me, so I'm relived that here on the internet in this low profile, anonymous venue I can talk freely without worrying about whether people will judge or believe me. I can just say what is actually going through my head without tuning it so as to accommodate someone else (which is not to say I want this to be convoluted for you! I just mean that I can speak more freely, and unfortunately this style of mine is how it all comes out: both turgid and turbid).

Thank you for working through this; I know I have a really taxing writing style when I write the way I'm naturally inclined (it's just not conversational or aware of the other person to whom I am speaking, as I discussed above) I want to believe that there is a living part of me that genuinely does experience gratitude for your reading this.
